articles.title: Bám đồng canh giữ chim trời
articles.text:
“Thiên la địa võng” trên đồng
Mới đây, vào sáng 25/9, trên cánh đồng thôn Hòa Mậu và Phước Tượng (xã Phú Lộc, TP. Huế), nhiều đàn cò trắng tìm về kiếm ăn. Tuy nhiên, lực lượng chức năng lại phát hiện hàng loạt điểm đặt bẫy với cò xốp và que dính nhựa được bố trí để dụ bắt chim trời trên những cánh đồng này vào mùa nước nổi.
Từ phản ánh của người dân và qua công tác nắm tình hình, Hạt Kiểm lâm khu vực phía Nam TP. Huế phối hợp Đồn Biên phòng Vinh Hiền, Công an, Ban Chỉ huy Quân sự xã Phú Lộc và Vườn Quốc gia Bạch Mã tổ chức kiểm tra, truy quét nạn tận diệt chim trời.
Chỉ trong vài giờ, lực lượng chức năng tháo dỡ, tiêu hủy khoảng 2.000 cò xốp và 8.000 que dính nhựa; đồng thời giải cứu 15 cá thể cò trắng mắc bẫy để thả về tự nhiên. Các đơn vị cũng khẩn trương vào cuộc xác minh người đặt số lượng lớn bẫy chim cùng dụng cụ dẫn dụ để xử lý theo quy định.
Đáng chú ý, đây không phải lần đầu các bẫy chim xuất hiện tại khu vực này. Sau nhiều đợt kiểm tra, truy quét, những chiếc lưới và cò xốp vẫn tiếp tục được dựng lên trên nhiều xứ đồng ở Huế.
Tình trạng tương tự diễn ra ở nhiều địa phương khác. Tại thôn Vĩnh Lương Khê (xã Phú Hồ), lợi dụng mùa chim di cư, các đối tượng chôn cọc tre, giăng lưới, đặt cò xốp để dẫn dụ chim. Qua kiểm tra, lực lượng chức năng tháo dỡ 500 m lưới, 35 cọc tre và giải cứu 8 cá thể chim mắc bẫy.
Trước đó, ngày 24/9, tại hai phường Thanh Thủy và Kim Long, lực lượng kiểm lâm phối hợp chính quyền địa phương tháo gỡ hàng trăm mét lưới cùng nhiều cọc tre, cò xốp, thiết bị phát tiếng chim. Hai ngày trước đó, tại phường Kim Trà, xã Quảng Điền và phường Hóa Châu, hơn 1.750 m lưới cùng nhiều dụng cụ bẫy chim cũng bị tháo dỡ, tiêu hủy.
Ven phá Tam Giang thuộc xã Đan Điền, lực lượng chức năng tiếp tục tháo gỡ 300 m lưới và 20 cọc tre. Tại xã Chân Mây - Lăng Cô, qua truy quét tại 3 địa điểm ở thôn An Cư Tây, các đơn vị chức năng thu giữ, tiêu hủy 650 cò mồi giả và 2.000 que dính nhựa. Riêng khu vực An Ninh Hạ (phường Kim Long), gần 3.000 m lưới cùng hàng trăm cọc tre và thiết bị phát tiếng chim bị tháo bỏ.
Giữ đất lành cho chim trời
Những vụ việc, con số kể trên cho thấy nạn bẫy bắt chim hoang dã tại Huế không còn xuất hiện đơn lẻ mà đã lan rộng từ vùng đồng ruộng ven trung tâm đô thị ra đến khu vực đầm phá, cửa biển.
Theo Chi cục Kiểm lâm TP. Huế, từ đầu năm đến nay, toàn thành phố đã tổ chức 38 đợt ra quân tháo dỡ bẫy chim. Qua đó, lực lượng chức năng tiêu hủy hơn 3.279 cò xốp, 15.179 que dính nhựa, 13.350 m lưới, 757 cọc tre giăng lưới, cùng nhiều loa, bình ắc quy, máy phát tiếng chim và bẫy kẹp. Có 135 cá thể chim trời được giải cứu, tái thả về môi trường tự nhiên.
Các cuộc ra quân xử lý nạn săn bắt chim trời được phối hợp giữa nhiều cơ quan, đơn vị, địa phương. Trong đó, lực lượng kiểm lâm giữ vai trò nòng cốt trong phát hiện, tháo dỡ các phương tiện bẫy bắt; công an tham gia xác minh, xử lý vi phạm; biên phòng, quân sự và chính quyền địa phương cùng tuần tra, truy quét, tuyên truyền tại cơ sở.
Ông Lê Ngọc Tuấn - Chi cục trưởng Chi cục Kiểm lâm TP. Huế, cho biết, mùa chim di cư cũng là lúc hoạt động bẫy bắt, mua bán, tiêu thụ chim hoang dã diễn biến phức tạp. Ngành kiểm lâm luôn tăng cường kiểm tra tại các khu vực có chim trời tập trung, tháo dỡ phương tiện bẫy bắt và phối hợp xác minh, xử lý vi phạm; đồng thời, tăng cường vận động người dân không săn bắt, mua bán, vận chuyển, tiêu thụ chim hoang dã và kịp thời xử lý hành vi vi phạm.
Theo ông Tuấn, bên cạnh các đợt truy quét, việc lực lượng kiểm lâm duy trì kiểm tra tại những địa điểm thường xuyên xuất hiện bẫy chim, với sự tham gia của chính quyền địa phương, cùng người dân, cộng đồng dân cư... có ý nghĩa quan trọng. Đây là cách hạn chế tình trạng vừa tháo dỡ hôm trước, hôm sau các dụng cụ bẫy bắt chim lại được tái lắp dựng.
Theo Chi cục Kiểm lâm TP. Huế, thời gian tới đơn vị tiếp tục phối hợp các cơ quan chức năng, địa phương tăng cường tuyên truyền, kiểm tra thực địa, tháo dỡ bẫy và xử lý các trường hợp săn bắt chim trái phép, góp phần giữ gìn sinh cảnh và tạo những vùng an toàn để chim trời trở về vào mỗi mùa di cư.

articles.title: How Biden Averted a War With Iran
articles.text: S hortly after Hamas’s October 7 attack on Israel, President Biden asked me to help lead negotiations for a cease-fire and hostage-release deal. After some initial progress, the talks soon stalled, as fighting raged in Gaza. On February 21, 2024, I went to Cairo to restart them, carrying a new proposal. Egypt’s intelligence headquarters is in northern Cairo, surrounded by leafy avenues. Behind its gates is the heartbeat of the formidable Egyptian security state. Abbas Kamel, the head of the intelligence service from 2018 to 2024, was one of the country’s most powerful figures, although little known. A reserved man in his 60s, he had served in military intelligence with Abdel Fattah el-Sisi, now Egypt’s president, and the two had remained close ever since. Kamel was also central to the effort to stop the war in Gaza through a hostage deal. His intelligence service maintained direct channels to Hamas’s leaders in Gaza. Seated beside me in his office, Kamel lit his third cigarette and signaled to his aide Ahmed Abdel Khalek to bring the Israelis into the room. “Now!” Kamel said. Abdel Khalek skirted out the door, clutching an ever-present binder of papers. Kamel, slumped in his chair, seemed at the end of his patience. The task of delivering Hamas to a hostage deal was proving impossible. But cigarettes had a calming effect on him. The routine of sparking a lighter; the long inhale. He’d lean back, his eyes following a cloud of smoke wafting toward a fan on the ceiling. Then he’d sit up with the hint of a smile, or a new idea. Time to take up smoking , I thought. Only three months earlier, Kamel and I had sat in this same room and helped close the first cease-fire deal of the war. For seven days in November, the fighting stopped. More than 100 hostages were freed—women and children, including toddlers and grandmothers—in exchange for hundreds of Palestinian prisoners held by Israel. Humanitarian aid surged into Gaza and, with the guns silent, reached those in need across the Strip. The deal collapsed when Hamas, at the last moment, refused to release the younger women it was holding. Hamas proposed that we skip over them and begin discussing the older men, a clear violation of the deal that we had put together over weeks of negotiations. This article is adapted from Brett McGurk’s new book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages . Israel refused. After midnight in Washington on December 1, 2023—early morning in Gaza—Hamas resumed firing rockets at Israel. Israel resumed air strikes. The war was back on. At the time, I had presumed that we’d succeed in putting together another deal, at least for the remaining women and the older men, including an American citizen. But Hamas held to maximalist demands. They included a return to the status quo of October 6, with the organization remaining in power in Gaza, reconstituted on the borders of Israel. After the massacres of October 7, when Hamas killed more than 1,000 and took more than 250 hostages, no Israeli leader would accept that outcome. [ Mark Bowden: The lesson of Israel’s success in the air ] Let alone Benjamin Netanyahu, Israel’s hard-line prime minister, who demanded as a war aim that Hamas be removed from power entirely. I would see him shortly after meeting Kamel. Our talks had further stalled as Iran ramped up attacks on Americans. In Iraq and Syria, U.S. troops came under near daily fire from Iranian-backed militias. Since October 7, these attacks had increased sevenfold from the year before, and the strikes aimed to kill. On Christmas Day, three Americans were wounded in a strike in northern Iraq, one grievously. Days later, the Iranian-backed proxy in Yemen, the Houthis, opened fire against ships in the Red Sea, including U.S. military vessels. The region was on the brink of a wider war. President Biden asked me to meet the Iranians in Oman, reactivating a back channel that had been used at times before the October 7 crisis. The day before my meeting, the Houthis launched their largest attack to date, firing about two dozen missiles and drones at U.S. and U.K. military ships. The back channel went nowhere. On January 28, 2024, two weeks after my meeting in Oman, an Iranian-supplied drone struck the living quarters of American troops in Jordan, killing three U.S. soldiers and wounding dozens. Biden finally chose to hit back, ordering the largest wave of air strikes across Iraq and Syria in more than a decade, including targeted strikes against the militia leader responsible for the attack in Jordan and the Iranian adviser in Baghdad enabling the militias. After that, the militias stood down. Now, finally, we were getting back to the hostage talks. Like Kamel, my patience was frayed. The war was now in its fifth month. Nearly 30,000 people had been reported killed in Gaza, including militants. More than 230 Israeli soldiers had died, and nearly 1,500 had been wounded. Hamas still held more than 100 hostages, including several American citizens. The carnage weighed on all of us. “We are mediators, Brett,” Kamel lamented. “It’s not my war, or your war; it’s their war, and they don’t want to stop. They both think they’ll win; there’s nothing to win.” He blew smoke to the ceiling. “They’ll destroy all of us, not just themselves.” The war could stop tomorrow with the release of six women hostages, I reminded him. These were the women passed over in the November deal, mostly civilians taken from a music festival. They’ll come last, he said. Hamas knew they were valuable to Israel. Kamel insisted that he was doing all he could, but we were stuck. Abdel Khalek returned with the Israeli delegation. Gaunt, with a military-style haircut graying like mine, Abdel Khalek was the Egyptian intelligence officer long charged with the Hamas file and was in direct contact with Yahya Sinwar, Hamas’s leader in Gaza and the mastermind of October 7. Few people outside Hamas knew the organization better. The Israeli delegation was led by Ronen Bar. With a shaved head and square jaw, Bar looked as if he’d stepped out of Fauda , the television drama about Shin Bet, the internal security agency he led. Bar was the main Israeli liaison with Hamas, and the Israeli official who most wanted a deal. He was willing to bend but not break Netanyahu’s guidance. To demonstrate his seriousness, Bar carried maps of Gaza rolled up in cases, and briefcases filled with the names of every Palestinian prisoner held by Israel, as well as all of the information Israel had on the hostages, their likely locations and conditions. Bar said Israel was prepared to finalize the details for an exchange of hostages for prisoners, down to the names of prisoners Hamas wanted released. He was also prepared to negotiate the conditions for a phased cease-fire, with Israeli forces withdrawing from Gaza to smaller perimeters as more hostages were freed by Hamas. If no hostages came out, Israeli forces would go in deeper. “That’s the formula,” Bar said. He challenged Kamel to convince Hamas to release at least one of the women. “I’m not Hamas!” Kamel said. Bar backtracked, meaning no offense. Rolling out a map in front of us, Bar explained that Israel was preparing a major military offensive in the southern Gaza city of Rafah. It would be the largest operation of the war so far. [ Arash Azizi: Iran is not ready for war with Israel ] Rafah was adjacent to Egypt’s border, and it was where Hamas remained militarily intact, still organized into brigades with subordinate battalions and smaller units beneath them. A network of tunnels deep underground fed into a main labyrinth to the north, known as the Kingdom, where Sinwar and his advisers had been hiding from Israeli forces, together with several hostages. Rafah was also where much of the civilian population had fled from Israel’s ongoing military operations elsewhere in Gaza. The only way to stop this planned operation, Bar said, was for Hamas to begin releasing hostages—starting with the women. Kamel said Hamas had opposite demands. Israel must withdraw completely from Gaza and guarantee a permanent cease-fire before it would release any hostages. Hamas and its leaders would remain in power, returning to the status quo of October 6. Meanwhile, Israel had to release all Palestinians held in Israeli prisons, regardless of crimes committed. That was Sinwar’s position, Kamel explained. “Impossible,” Bar said. He looked at me, wondering why I had recommended this meeting. “What is this?” he asked. In a negotiation with irreconcilable views, a mediator tries to create a “zone of possible agreement.” Between Hamas and Israel, there was none whatsoever. “Let’s consider a different approach,” I said. Together with Bill Burns, the CIA director and my partner in the hostage negotiations, I had developed a compromise framework to overcome the impasse. It would focus first on an area where both sides might agree: a cease-fire and the release of large numbers of Palestinian prisoners in exchange for a humanitarian category of hostages, starting with the remaining women and the older men, and then the sick or wounded. There were more than 30 hostages in those categories, including three Americans. The incentive for Hamas was a prolonged cease-fire—at least six weeks, longer than what was promised for the remaining women alone. And it could continue as long as talks continued for the remaining hostages, creating a chance to last a year or more. Bar said the Israeli side could accept that outline. Kamel smashed the butt of his cigarette in an ashtray. “They have greater demands,” he said. “You both know this. Sinwar won’t agree—” “Then push them! Push them!” Bar interrupted. “I do!” Kamel said. “What about you? Push Netanyahu!” I raised my arms to stop the two men from shouting at each other. Kamel retreated: “I trust you, Ronen. I trust you. But what does Netanyahu say?” Bar insisted that he was speaking for Netanyahu. “We need to hear it from your prime minister.” I was seeing Netanyahu the following day. “He’ll agree,” I predicted. “Release our girls, the war stops,” Bar insisted. We stood and shook hands. The three of us had no choice but to work together. Kamel asked Abdel Khalek to join us. “We’ll do our best,” Kamel said. Abdel Khalek shrugged, looking unconvinced. “Inshallah, inshallah,” he said. T he first thing a visitor to the prime minister’s office in Jerusalem sees is a wall draped with a map of Africa and the Middle East, with Israel, the size of a postage stamp, in the middle. Netanyahu greeted me in front of the map, then posed for a photo with a smile. Once the press had left the room, he offered his own bleak assessment of things across the map. Northern Israel had been evacuated. More than 80,000 people had relocated to escape daily rocket fire from Hezbollah in Lebanon. Southern Israel, the areas near Gaza, had also been evacuated, up to 50,000 people. Nearly 5 percent of Israeli territory was now a no-man’s-land. Netanyahu likened Hamas’s insistence on restoring its positions on Israel’s borders to national suicide. Israel won’t be a country, he said. People would never return to areas bordering Hamas or Hezbollah. His priority was creating the conditions for people to return home. In the south, that meant Hamas would never again exist adjacent to Israel. In the north, if a deal was reached in Gaza, he’d leave Hezbollah alone for now. If not, then Israel might have to clear Hezbollah from that border too. For more than 30 minutes, he never mentioned the hostages. “I’m here to discuss the hostage deal,” I reminded him. Netanyahu by this time was under criticism for not prioritizing the release of hostages over the military campaign inside Gaza. The criticism seemed valid. He was animated in discussing the military campaign, and far less so when discussing the hostages—when he chose to discuss them at all. He believed that it was only through a military campaign that Israel could secure the release of the hostages. There could not be one without the other. “So, how’s that all going?” Netanyahu asked me. “Not great, it seems.” I explained where we stood. The aim was to unite around the proposal we had discussed in Cairo, with Israel signed on and endorsed by Qatar and Egypt. “That places the onus squarely on Sinwar,” I said. “Why don’t you ask Hamas to accept something, then come to me,” Netanyahu said. This was not the way to negotiate with Hamas, he insisted. The group would pocket anything Israel accepted and then keep demanding more. “You’re doing things backward,” he said. [ David Frum: A test of strength ] Netanyahu also believed that time was on his side, not Sinwar’s. Israeli forces had finally discovered the Kingdom, thought to be the heart of Hamas’s extensive tunnel system. There, they had found millions of dollars in cash, along with Sinwar’s handwritten notes, laptops, and phones. Hamas’s leader had left the area before Israeli forces arrived, but they were now thought to be closing in. Eliminating Sinwar, combined with the looming Rafah operation, Netanyahu thought, would force Hamas to soften its demands and give up all the hostages, not just some. In the end, Netanyahu told me that he’d accept our proposal—a six-week cease-fire and a release of Palestinian prisoners in exchange for the women, elderly, and ill hostages—in principle. But the constant rounds of talks were grating on him, because they seemed to treat Hamas leaders as statesmen, as opposed to terrorists holding hostages in tunnels. “It won’t work,” he said. I agreed that eliminating Sinwar would be important and might help unlock a hostage deal, but until that happened, we should work to corner him—militarily and diplomatically. I called Abdel Khalek after the meeting. There was still no word from Hamas. I told him that Netanyahu accepted the proposal in principle. But even after spending nearly two hours with the prime minister, I could not be sure. Netanyahu was just impossible to pin down. Was he aiming to sabotage the talks, or was it his genuine view that Sinwar would only release the hostages with a knife to his throat? Until that proposition was tested, it was impossible to know. T wo weeks later , Hamas’s response to our proposal reinforced Netanyahu’s view that negotiations were going nowhere. The group rejected the compromise deal and stuck to its original demands. On March 18, Biden called Netanyahu and urged him to sweeten the deal by offering to release a larger number of Palestinian prisoners. Netanyahu reluctantly agreed, but Hamas would not budge. A week later, the United Nations Security Council voted on a resolution calling for an unconditional cease-fire in Gaza during the month of Ramadan, which was about to begin. The U.S. abstained from the vote, allowing the resolution to pass. Our UN team thought it would be too reputationally costly to veto it, as we had done with previous resolutions calling for an unconditional cease-fire—meaning without any hostages being freed. Ron Dermer, a member of Netanyahu’s cabinet who was formerly Israel’s ambassador to the U.S., called me after the vote. He said Hamas had praised the resolution and asked why our administration treated Israel as a “dishrag” at the UN. The charge was offensive, given Biden’s staunch support for Israel, and I told him as much, hanging up the phone. But while Dermer’s rhetoric was overheated, he was not wrong that Hamas saw the UN resolution as a strategic opening to strengthen its position. The day after the vote, Hamas’s leadership met with Iran’s supreme leader, Ayatollah Khamenei, in Tehran, and pointed to Israel’s growing international isolation. The Houthis escalated their missile and drone attacks in the Red Sea. And with no progress in sight, Israeli negotiators withdrew from the talks altogether. “Israel will not surrender to Hamas’s delusional demands,” Netanyahu said in a statement. Our efforts to stop the war through a hostage deal were dead. Meanwhile, Biden was under political pressure at home—mainly from within his own party—to somehow force Israel to stop the war. Earlier in March, the journalist Jonathan Capehart had asked Biden whether Israel’s planned offensive in Rafah was a “red line,” given the potential impact on civilians. “It is a red line,” Biden said, adding that Israel “must pay more attention to the innocent lives being lost.” Biden later told us that he was referring to how Israel should conduct the operation, not whether it was conducted at all. In the same interview, he said he was “never going to leave Israel.” Around the same time, however, Vice President Harris told ABC News that Israel’s operation in Rafah would be a “huge mistake” and refused to rule out “consequences” if it went ahead. Looking back, it’s no wonder that Hamas never responded to our proposals during this period. We now know that in March 2024, as this political debate was taking place in the U.S., Sinwar was in a tunnel complex underneath Rafah. An avid consumer of news, he would have understood that relations between Biden and Netanyahu were approaching the boiling point. A year later, Ronen Bar visited Washington, D.C., and met with a group of former Biden aides. One of them asked plaintively what Biden should have done differently in the negotiations with Hamas. Bar pointed to this period in spring 2024, when Biden was said to be blocking Israel’s operation in Rafah. From Bar’s vantage point, that perception had hardened Hamas’s position, making it more difficult to free the hostages and end the war. “That was your biggest mistake,” he said. O n the morning of April 1 , a group of Israeli officials crowded into the White House Situation Room to lay out their humanitarian plans for the Rafah operation. Following Biden’s comments, we had made clear that the operation should not begin before civilians had the opportunity to leave the area. Before the meeting started, Israel’s ambassador, Michael Herzog, and its military attaché, Major General Hidai Zilberman, asked to speak with me outside the room, so as not to be overheard. Zilberman said that Israel was about to conduct an air strike in Damascus. The target was Mohammad Reza Zahedi, a senior Iranian officer responsible for proxy operations across Syria and Lebanon, including Hezbollah. That was not particularly surprising. Zahedi was a legitimate target for the Israelis, given the ongoing Hezbollah attacks in northern Israel. I thanked Zilberman for informing me. [ The Editors: The Biden doctrine ] “One more thing,” he said. He was a giant man with a shaved head, resembling a heavyweight boxer, and his large dome leaned toward mine. Iran might claim that the building about to be attacked was a consulate, Zilberman said, but it was not. I pressed him: Diplomatic facilities are protected under international law. If the target in Damascus was a consulate, it was off-limits. Zilberman insisted that the Israelis had seen no evidence that was the case. By the time we got out of the meeting, the building had been flattened and Zahedi and several of his associates were dead. Iran declared that it viewed the strike as an attack on Iranian territory and vowed to strike Israel in retaliation. We soon picked up reports that Iran was preparing for a missile attack against Israeli cities. It was hard to believe at first. For decades, Iran had fought using proxies, allowing itself some deniability and reducing the risk of retaliatory attacks inside its own borders. But more reports came in showing preparations for a massive strike—a combination of ballistic missiles, cruise missiles, and drones aimed at hundreds of targets across Israel. In urgent consultations with the Israelis, we calculated how many defensive missile interceptors would be needed in a worst-case scenario. Israel has some of the world’s most sophisticated air defenses, including Arrow systems that target missiles at the edge of outer space and closer-range defenses that take out lesser threats. But based on what we were seeing from Iran, even that capability might not be enough. Zilberman visited my office with a formal request for U.S. military forces to help defend Israeli territory—air wings, destroyers, and missile defenses. The request was extraordinary, and it broke with Israel’s traditional doctrine: We defend ourselves, by ourselves. When I told Biden’s chief of staff, Jeff Zients, and other top White House aides that we might be about to see the largest ballistic-missile attack in history, with Israel as the target, they were visibly alarmed—both for the people who lived there and for how it might affect the 2024 election. The focus in the West Wing had shifted to the campaign, and Biden’s team wanted him to appear strong and in command, not captive to events. Biden was determined to defend Israel, but his frustration with the crisis—and with Netanyahu—was growing. The president was known for picking up the phone at all hours—he once called my mother out of the blue. But in the first quarter of 2024, he spoke with Netanyahu only a handful of times, compared with nearly 20 calls in the last quarter of 2023. Relations between the two leaders deteriorated further after Senate Majority Leader Chuck Schumer called for Israel to hold elections and replace Netanyahu. Netanyahu believed that Biden had put Schumer up to it; Biden denied this, but later called Schumer’s remarks a “good speech.” Late in the day on April 1, hours after Israel’s attack in Damascus, an Israeli drone struck a convoy in northern Gaza and killed seven aid workers affiliated with World Central Kitchen, a nonprofit led by the chef José Andrés. The Israelis had welcomed Andrés and his organization into Gaza, viewing them as more trustworthy than the U.N. The strike was a tragedy—Israel called it a “grave mistake”—and it fueled calls for an immediate and unconditional cease-fire. Biden was now being criticized from all sides: The left saw him as too weak to rein in Israel, while the right saw him as too weak to force Hamas to free the hostages and, more broadly, as having no articulable plan to end the war. Against this backdrop, Biden and Netanyahu spoke on April 4. The all-out Middle East war that the U.S. had sought to avoid was fast approaching. Iran had hundreds of ballistic missiles and drones aimed at Israel. Israel was planning a counterattack. The hostage talks with Hamas were dead. The humanitarian crisis in Gaza was worsening. When I walked into the Oval Office that day, Biden’s face was red like a beet. I sat in front of his desk with a larger crowd than usual, including Zients, Secretary of State Antony Blinken, and Burns. Everyone sensed that something was about to give. “What the fuck am I telling this guy?” Biden asked. There were different views. Some people advised the president to simply tell Netanyahu that the war was over; if he refused, we’d cut Israel’s support. Biden was hearing this sentiment on the campaign trail from parts of the Democratic Party. But he asked what would happen if we cut military assistance while hostages remained in tunnels and the war continued, with Israel under attack from multiple directions. “We’re on the side of Iran?” he asked rhetorically. Burns advised that a hostage deal remained the only path to a cease-fire. That meant maintaining support for Israel while trying to restart the negotiations with Hamas and easing the immense human suffering in Gaza as much as possible. I agreed with Burns but chose not to say much, taking in the scene and trying to read Biden, who seemed ready to blow his stack. Jake Sullivan, the national security adviser, discussed Israel’s preparations for the missile attack and its request for U.S. military support. On Biden’s desk were orders, recommended by Secretary of Defense Lloyd Austin, for the emergency deployment of additional forces to the region. Biden said he approved them, without hesitation. He then asked how we might return to the hostage deal. It seemed hopeless, but Burns suggested that there might be an opportunity to use Iran’s attack to our advantage. If we helped defeat it, Netanyahu would owe us, and Sinwar would see that even a direct attack by Iran could not improve Hamas’s position. “If we don’t defeat it?” Biden asked, unconvinced. The answer was regional war. Israel had already prepared a counterattack in the event that Iran’s missiles caused Israeli casualties. “Great,” Biden said. The Situation Room connected the call. Biden jumped in. “Bibi, man, what the fuck are you doing?” He gripped the phone tight. “You think I’m Santa Claus? No Santa in Israel, pal.” When Netanyahu asked what he meant, Biden said he could cut off military aid to Israel with the snap of a finger, leaving the country on its own. Netanyahu retorted that Israel would defend itself even without the United States. (We later learned that he concluded from this call that we were cutting military supplies.) [ Franklin Foer: How Netanyahu lost America ] Returning to his prepared points, Biden made specific requests regarding humanitarian aid and opening additional crossings into northern Gaza. Netanyahu began to discuss Israel’s preliminary assessment of the strike on the aid workers, claiming that it was more complicated than what was being reported in the news—a tragic miscommunication. Biden interrupted: “I don’t want to hear it, Bibi.” He said he’d help defend Israel against Iran, but then the U.S. would move immediately to end the war and free the hostages. “That’s the deal, pal.” He hung up abruptly. It was a short call. If not for the pending Iranian attack, the U.S. might have taken irreversible measures against Israel at this juncture. My own mind wrestled with whether this might have been a better course. We all wanted the war to end. It was a sickening horror in every dimension. Was the means to that end the hostage and cease-fire deal—the course we had been on—or simply telling Israel to stop, even as it was under attack on multiple fronts? If there was a better way to end the crisis, Biden would have taken it. He had tried a UN resolution calling for an unconditional cease-fire. He had tried increasing public pressure. Those steps only seemed to make the situation worse. There were multiple belligerents in this conflict. Increasing public pressure on Israel did not stop the war. It seemed to encourage those fighting against it. I had never seen Biden so frustrated—spitting mad, literally. Sullivan took out a note card to draft the readout, the official summary of the call. We debated whether to publicly threaten to cut military aid to Israel. Biden was not comfortable doing so at a moment when hundreds of Iranian missiles were being readied for launch. The final readout warned that U.S. policy “will be determined by our assessment of Israel’s immediate action” on “specific, concrete, and measurable steps to address civilian harm, humanitarian suffering, and the safety of aid workers.” At the same time, it said that Biden had “made clear that the United States strongly supports Israel in the face of [Iran’s] threats.” This was the paradox. For all Biden’s frustration with the situation, and with Netanyahu, Israel was under attack from common enemies. Fueling Iran’s confidence was the belief that Biden was under pressure to break with Israel. Iran seemed to believe that a missile attack against Israel might help push Biden over the edge. That proved to be a miscalculation. O n Saturday, April 13 , Biden took his seat at the head of the table in the Situation Room. He’d just come from his home in Rehoboth Beach, Delaware, and had two shirt buttons undone beneath his jacket. I had been at the White House since early in the morning to help coordinate Israel’s defense with other countries in the region. Iran’s attack began around 3:30 p.m. with 200 drones, followed 90 minutes later by 30 cruise missiles. Those were all in the air and flying toward Israel by the time Biden arrived. The ballistic missiles had yet to launch. The flight time for drones from Iran to Israel was three hours. Cruise missiles took about half that time, and ballistic missiles took 13 minutes. Iran’s launch sequence ensured that all of the attacks would converge on Israel at the same moment. The aim was to overwhelm Israeli air defenses and allow the heavy-payload ballistic missiles to hit their targets. Earlier that day, Tehran had sent a message warning that if the U.S. helped defend Israel, it could no longer restrain militias in Iraq and Syria, which had not fired a shot against U.S. personnel since our air strikes in February. Meanwhile, Herzog and Zilberman had visited my office to review Israel’s potential response to an Iranian attack. If Iran’s missiles killed Israelis, Zilberman said, then Iran had no idea what was coming. His large fist pounded my desk. Seated in the Situation Room with Biden were Austin, Blinken, Sullivan, Chairman of the Joint Chiefs General C. Q. Brown, and other senior advisers. Harris was on a video feed from Los Angeles. General Erik Kurilla, overseeing U.S. operations, was on video from his headquarters in Tampa, Florida. Biden asked about our preparations. Over the previous 96 hours, the U.S. had strengthened defenses in and around Israel, deployed military assets and fighter squadrons, and coordinated with a makeshift coalition of Arab and European states. “Good as we could do,” Austin said. “Where’s Bibi?” Biden asked. Netanyahu was in an underground command center in Israel, where he planned to ride out the attack and then determine how to respond. Burns sketched out possible scenarios. If Iran’s attacks killed Israelis, Israel would launch a large air attack on Iran. This would bring a state-on-state conflict to the Middle East for the first time in decades, with the risk of drawing in the U.S. Biden said he would not allow that to happen. We may not have a choice , I thought. Kurilla reported that American air squadrons were taking down dozens of slow-flying Iranian drones over Syria, Iraq, and Saudi Arabia. He called it a turkey shoot. One of those pilots was Lieutenant Colonel Kevin Murphy. Days earlier, he had been at home in North Carolina, he later recalled in Air & Space Forces Magazine . He arrived in the Middle East less than 24 hours before it became the largest aerial combat zone since the Korean War. Murphy and his weapons officer, Major George Welton, along with the rest of their squadron, shot down two dozen drones. Defeating these first salvos was critical for saving the main air defenses for the ballistic-missile attack. “Ballistic missiles could be the challenge,” Austin said. Iran’s ballistic missiles could descend at speeds of 5,000 miles per hour, striking targets with precision while carrying a 1,000-pound warhead. U.S. and Israeli air-defense systems are the best in the world, but if Iran launched enough missiles, it was a near certainty that some would get through and reach their targets. In the eastern Mediterranean, American destroyers readied in coordination with Israeli land-based defenses. Patriot anti-missile batteries operated by the U.S. Army stood by across the Middle East, from Iraq to Jordan, scanning the skies for targets. “What’s your worst case?” Biden asked. Nobody knew for sure how many missiles the Iranians might shoot at once. The worst-case scenario was thought to be 50 or more. “So we just wait?” Biden asked. Heads nodded. The screen on the wall in front of me suddenly showed yellow streaks rising from Iran. Kurilla opened his mic: “Mr. President, Mr. Secretary, we have confirmed ballistic-missile launches. Thirty launches total from tracks.” “We can handle 30,” Austin said. The streaks rose from across Iran and built up speed as they approached the edge of the atmosphere. Kurilla, moments later: “Thirty new launches, Mr. President.” “Thirty new launches?” Biden asked. Kurilla confirmed that there were now 60 missiles in the air. More yellow streaks rose from Iran as the first wave curved horizontally across Iraq, heading for targets in Israel. “That’s a challenge,” Austin said. “Six minutes before defenses engage,” Kurilla said. I had never felt so helpless in this room, the command center of the most powerful country on Earth. I knew what interceptors we would fire first, the backups if they failed—everything that was about to transpire. Yet, for the first time ever while seated at that table, I bowed my head and prayed. More yellow lines rose from the digital map of Iran. Kurilla confirmed a third salvo. Ninety missiles were now in the air, coming in three waves. “I’m dropping to coordinate defense,” he said. “Ninety?” Biden said. Moments later, more streaks. I couldn’t believe my eyes. Kurilla confirmed a fourth salvo. There were now more than 100 ballistic missiles flying toward Israel. Nobody said a word. Many, like me, were seemingly in quiet prayer. [ Andrew Exum: Netanyahu doesn’t care about his friendship with Biden ] Four minutes before the missiles reached the range of our defenses, the room was so quiet that you could hear a digital red clock humming on the wall. Then streaks appeared from the other side of the screen: interceptors launching from Israel and our destroyers at sea, and Patriots from elsewhere. Israel’s Arrows built speed to Mach 9, more than one mile per second. American destroyers fired SM-3 interceptors that traveled even faster, reaching incoming missiles above the atmosphere in tens of seconds. Screens across three walls tracked hundreds of converging missiles and interceptors, like a multiplayer video game. It did not seem real. Suddenly, bright-white flashes burst onto the screens: Satellite imaging was picking up the interceptors as they exploded 60 miles above the Earth. “Defenses engaged,” Kurilla said, stating the obvious. The entire Middle East, from Israel to Lebanon, Syria, and Jordan, was covered in apocalyptic white airbursts. Through his cockpit window 6,000 miles from the White House, Murphy saw interceptors launch to engage missiles far above him. There were massive explosions in all directions, then wreckage descending around his aircraft. “You fly through it,” he recalled. “You think skinny, you pray, and you continue on the heading that you’re on.” “Impacts?” Biden asked. Reports incoming, Kurilla said. “We won’t know straightaway,” Brown added. The door opened. A watch officer delivered a note from Nate Swanson, my lead adviser on Iran. It was a message from the Iranians, saying that what was in the air now was the end of the attack, but that they would launch a larger salvo if Israel responded. I read the note to Biden. He nodded, too much information coming in at once. The screens gradually cleared. All of the missiles had either reached their targets or been intercepted. There was nothing to indicate what had happened at ground level. “Erik, report,” Austin said. Kurilla answered that we had no confirmed impacts in Israel. The defenses appeared to have been successful. Many in the Situation Room leaned back in their chairs with sighs of relief. “Thank God,” someone said. I remained on edge. “We won’t know for certain yet,” Austin warned. Kurilla again: “Israelis confirm no significant impacts.” “Pretty good,” Austin said quietly. “Unless Iran fires more.” “They claim they won’t,” I said. Biden nodded to Sullivan. “Get Bibi on the line.” “What do you want to say to him?” I asked. “I just saved his ass, that’s what. Cut this off here.” “Take the win,” Sullivan added. Outside the room, I connected with the Israelis in their bunker. Netanyahu asked for 30 minutes before taking the call, which further riled up Biden. “Does he know we just saved his ass?” Biden asked. This was the first time the U.S. military—let alone the U.S. military together with a coalition of European and Arab countries—had fought to defend Israel. The moment was not lost on Biden. Now the question was how to leverage it. Sullivan recommended that we use the time to craft what Biden would say to Netanyahu. “Go,” the president said. “Hurry up.” Deputy National Security Adviser Jon Finer and I went with Sullivan to his office and huddled behind his desk as he typed out talking points. For the key takeaway, we chose to use Sullivan’s formulation (“Take the win”) instead of Biden’s (“I just saved your ass”). We recommended that the president ask Israel to respond in a way that inflicted few casualties and aimed to end the direct exchange of fire. Then we would get back to the hostage deal. Netanyahu was ready for the call. Back in the Situation Room, we handed Biden a draft. He read it aloud, made a few adjustments, and said, “Put him on.” Netanyahu’s voice came through the speakers: “Hi, Joe, quite a night here.” “Looks like you’ve come out okay, Bibi.” By this time, only one casualty had been confirmed, a young girl wounded by falling shrapnel in southern Israel. “I’m still getting reports, but yes, the good news is the defenses worked.” “ Our defenses, Bibi—” “Joe, we worked together, our militaries and our teams. It’s historic. Unbelievable, a coalition of militaries; I know it. But, Joe, the lesson is that these maniacs are willing to fire hundreds of missiles at Israel–this has never been done before, nowhere.” The lesson was that Israel needed the United States, Biden pressed. “Against these maniacs from Iran; they’re your enemies too,” Netanyahu said. “Take the win,” Biden said abruptly. He explained that Israel had every right to respond, but the response should be developed with us and designed to deter, not escalate. Take your time and get it right, he urged. Netanyahu was noncommittal. He had to see what the light of day brought to Israel. “We need to teach these maniacs a lesson,” he said. Biden again pressed Bibi to take the win and work with us on a response. He said our military team would coordinate with Netanyahu’s. “Let’s have our teams discuss it,” Netanyahu said. They agreed to talk again soon. The call dropped. Biden turned back to us with his palms up, asking for our views. “He heard you,” Sullivan said. Austin said he’d work with the Israelis on response options. It was approaching 10 p.m., with a long night ahead. We soon received another message from Iran, warning us again not to support Israel. Then a public message from Iran’s UN mission in New York: “US MUST STAY AWAY!!” For the first time since October 7, I thought, Tehran seemed anxious. The following morning, Biden spoke with the pilots and air commanders responsible for the defense, including Murphy and Welton’s squadron. He expressed gratitude as commander in chief for what they had just done. “It’s what we train for, sir,” said one of the pilots. “I don’t think you ever trained for last night,” Biden said. “There’s never been anything like it. The only reason we’re not in a major war right now is because of what you did. I mean it, guys. Thank you, thank you, thank you. You saved the world; I mean it. God bless you.” This article is adapted from Brett McGurk’s new book, Brink: Inside the Race to Free the October 7th Hostages .

articles.title: Được miễn học phí, học sinh TPHCM vẫn phải tốn bao nhiêu tiền mỗi tháng?
articles.text:
Đủ khoản phải lo
Dù học phí được miễn, nhưng trên thực tế, phụ huynh vẫn có thể phát sinh thêm nhiều khoản chi cho việc ăn bán trú, đưa đón, chăm sóc học sinh và các dịch vụ, chương trình theo nhu cầu.
Gia đình anh Đ.N., có con học tại một trường khu trung tâm TPHCM, cho biết năm học này nhà trường chưa công bố đầy đủ các khoản phải đóng. Tuy nhiên, nếu đối chiếu với bảng thu của năm học trước, gia đình dự kiến mỗi tháng vẫn phải chi hơn 2 triệu đồng cho các khoản phục vụ việc học và sinh hoạt của con tại trường.
Năm ngoái, mỗi tháng, vị phụ huynh này phải đóng hơn 2 triệu đồng cho các khoản ở trường của con. Phần lớn khoản chi dành cho tiền ăn, bán trú và các dịch vụ phục vụ học sinh trong ngày. Ngoài ra còn có các chương trình ngoại ngữ, kỹ năng sống, STEM, câu lạc bộ...
"Tính bình quân, gia đình tôi phải chi khoảng 2,4 triệu đồng mỗi tháng cho các khoản tại trường, dù không có dòng học phí. Tôi có 2 cháu đang đi học, cũng tốn gần 5 triệu, chưa tính sách vở, đồng phục, dụng cụ học tập. Chi phí này cũng là khoản lớn với gia đình tôi", anh N. bày tỏ.
Tương tự, một gia đình khác có con học THCS tại phường Tân Mỹ (TPHCM) cũng chi mỗi tháng gần 2 triệu đồng. Ngoài tiền ăn bán trú, gia đình còn đăng ký một số chương trình như ngoại ngữ với người nước ngoài, tin học quốc tế, STEM, kỹ năng sống, lớp năng khiếu... nên tổng số tiền phát sinh cao hơn so với những học sinh chỉ sử dụng các dịch vụ cơ bản.
Tuy vậy, tổng số tiền mỗi gia đình chi cho việc học của con có thể khác nhau, tùy vào dịch vụ học sinh sử dụng tại trường. Với những học sinh không sử dụng dịch vụ bán trú, tổng các khoản phải đóng sẽ giảm đáng kể, nhưng phụ huynh vẫn có thể chi thêm khoảng 500.000 đồng đến 1 triệu đồng mỗi tháng cho các chương trình như ngoại khóa, tiếng Anh tăng cường và các dịch vụ theo nhu cầu.
Phụ huynh được biết và được chọn đến đâu?
Theo hướng dẫn của Sở GD&ĐT TPHCM, các khoản thu ngoài học phí gồm nhiều nhóm dịch vụ phục vụ, hỗ trợ hoạt động giáo dục, chương trình nhà trường ngoài giờ chính khóa và các khoản theo nhu cầu của học sinh.
Trong đó, nhiều khoản đã được quy định mức trần. Với dịch vụ ăn uống, suất ăn sáng có mức 20.000 đồng/học sinh/ngày; suất ăn trưa, ăn xế tối đa 40.000 đồng/học sinh/ngày; nước uống 20.000 đồng/học sinh/tháng.
Các hoạt động ngoại khóa tối đa 200.000 đồng/học sinh/hoạt động; kỹ năng sống từ 80.000-120.000 đồng/học sinh/tháng; học bơi an toàn, phòng chống đuối nước tối đa 700.000 đồng/học sinh/khóa.
Trường hợp sử dụng máy lạnh, mức thu tối đa 35.000-50.000 đồng/học sinh/tháng đối với lớp đã được trang bị và 90.000-110.000 đồng/học sinh/tháng với lớp có nhu cầu nhưng chưa có máy lạnh. Tiền giữ xe học sinh, cha mẹ học sinh cũng có mức trần, từ 2.000 đồng/lượt hoặc 40.000 đồng/tháng đối với xe đạp, xe đạp điện và 4.000 đồng/lượt hoặc 80.000 đồng/tháng đối với xe máy, xe máy điện.
Theo Sở GD&ĐT TPHCM, các mức trên là mức tối đa. Nhà trường vẫn phải căn cứ nhu cầu thực tế, lập dự toán và xác định mức thu phù hợp, không được vượt mức trần quy định.
Bên cạnh đó, những chương trình như ngoại ngữ, STEM, câu lạc bộ và các hoạt động ngoài chương trình chính khóa phải dựa trên nhu cầu đăng ký của học sinh, phụ huynh và được tổ chức ngoài thời gian học chính khóa. Với các khoản thu hộ để mua đồng phục, học phẩm, học liệu, nhà trường cũng phải có sự đồng thuận của phụ huynh.
Sở GD&ĐT TPHCM yêu cầu các trường công khai các khoản thu, phát hành biên lai, hóa đơn và tránh thu dồn nhiều khoản cùng thời điểm. Những phần chi phí đã được ngân sách hoặc nguồn khác hỗ trợ phải được trừ khi xác định mức thu. Nếu cuối năm số tiền thu từ dịch vụ cao hơn chi phí thực tế, phần chênh lệch phải được hoàn trả cho học sinh.

articles.title: ĐBQH: Cần thận trọng khi mở rộng quyền sử dụng biển cho tổ chức, cá nhân
articles.text:
Chiều 28/9, phát biểu thảo luận tại Hội nghị đại biểu Quốc hội chuyên trách lần thứ Nhất, góp ý Dự án Luật Tài nguyên, môi trường biển và hải đảo (sửa đổi), ĐBQH Trần Văn Lâm (Bắc Ninh) cho biết dự thảo Luật lần này đã thể hiện nhiều thay đổi quan trọng, thể hiện tư duy mới trong quản lý. Đây đều là những hướng tiếp cận phù hợp với nhu cầu phát triển mới.
Tuy nhiên, đại biểu đã dành toàn bộ thời gian phát biểu của mình để đề nghị xem xét việc mở rộng quyền sử dụng biển cho tổ chức và cá nhân.
Nêu lý do, đại biểu cho rằng chúng ta đã có bài học thực tiễn rất lớn trong quản lý đất đai. Hiện nay, việc Nhà nước giao quyền sử dụng đất cho hộ gia đình, cá nhân, tổ chức đã tạo động lực rất lớn cho phát triển. Quyền sử dụng đất đã trở thành nguồn lực cho sản xuất kinh doanh, đầu tư, vay vốn tín dụng.
Nhưng cùng với thời gian, quyền sử dụng đất ngày càng mang tính tài sản và có thể chuyển nhượng, thế chấp, góp vốn. Thị trường cũng phát sinh rất nhiều các quan hệ phức tạp như đầu cơ, tích tụ chờ tăng giá, chuyển mục đích để hưởng chênh lệch địa tô, tranh chấp, định giá, thu hồi, bồi thường, đấu giá bỏ cọc, sử dụng đất không đúng mục đích, khiếu nại, tố cáo phức tạp phát sinh rất nhiều.
Theo đại biểu, một khu vực biển còn phức tạp hơn nhiều so với một thửa đất. Bởi một thửa đất thông thường chỉ có ranh giới tương đối ổn định, nhưng một khu vực biển là không gian ba chiều; cùng một vị trí có thể liên quan đến mặt nước, khối nước, đáy biển, lòng đất dưới đáy biển, đồng thời có thể ảnh hưởng đến luồng hàng hải, nguồn lợi thủy sản, điện gió, dầu khí, quốc phòng, môi trường, sinh kế của cộng đồng. Do đó, tính chất phức tạp của nguồn lực tài nguyên biển là lớn hơn.
Theo ông, kinh nghiệm từ đất đai đặt ra ít nhất ba bài toán cần phải được làm rõ ngay từ khi thiết kế luật này.
Một là, phải xác định thật rõ bản chất và giới hạn về quyền sử dụng khu vực biển. Quyền này không được hiểu gần như quyền sở hữu, cũng không nên cơ học sao chép toàn bộ các quyền của người sử dụng đất.
Cùng với đó, cần phân biệt rõ quyền nào được chuyển nhượng, quyền nào được thế chấp, góp vốn, cho thuê lại; trường hợp nào phải được Nhà nước chấp thuận; khu vực nào thuộc quốc phòng, an ninh, môi trường hoặc lợi ích chiến lược phải hạn chế giao dịch.
Điều quan trọng là không để sau này hình thành tình trạng được giao biển nhưng mục đích, mục tiêu chính lại là giữ quyền chờ tăng giá. Người được giao biển phải có đủ năng lực, có dự án, có tiến độ và phải đưa khu vực biển vào sử dụng đúng mục đích, hiệu quả.
Hai là, đặc biệt kiểm soát việc chuyển mục đích sử dụng biển và phần giá trị tăng thêm do quyết định của Nhà nước. Nếu như với đất đai, một quyết định thay đổi quy hoạch hay chuyển mục đích cũng có thể làm giá trị quyền sử dụng tăng lên rất lớn, thì với biển tình huống tương tự hoàn toàn có thể xảy ra.
Một khu vực ban đầu được giao cho hoạt động có giá trị thấp, sau đó chuyển sang cảng biển, năng lượng, du lịch và hoạt động thương mại thì giá trị sẽ tăng lên rất nhiều lần.
Vì vậy, cần làm rõ ngay từ đầu việc chuyển mục đích không phải là quyền đương nhiên của người đang sử dụng. Khi thay đổi mục đích làm tăng căn bản giá trị kinh tế của khu vực biển thì nghĩa vụ tài chính phải được xác định lại.
"Cần thiết phải xem xét cơ chế lựa chọn nhà đầu tư, nếu không kiểm soát tốt khâu này thì sẽ hình thành cơ chế để hưởng lợi từ mục đích khác", đại biểu góp ý.
Ba là, quản lý toàn bộ hồ sơ quyền sử dụng biển bằng dữ liệu số, công khai, minh bạch ngay từ đầu. Thực tế cho thấy, đất đai hiện nay phải xử lý rất nhiều các quan hệ lịch sử qua nhiều thời kỳ nhưng chưa đăng ký hồ sơ và thực tế sử dụng rất khác nhau.
Theo ông Lâm, đối với biển, chúng ta đang xây dựng một chế định mới nên có điều kiện tránh lặp lại vấn đề đó. Việc giao, cho thuê, đăng ký, chuyển nhượng, thế chấp, thay đổi chủ thể, chuyển mục đích và thu hồi quyền sử dụng khu vực biển, cần được cập nhật vào hệ thống dữ liệu thống nhất.
"Một khu vực biển phải được xác định ngay: Ai đang sử dụng, sử dụng vào mục đích gì, trong thời hạn bao lâu và nghĩa vụ tài chính thế nào, có đang thế chấp hay chuyển nhượng hay không.
Đồng thời phải thiết kế rõ cơ chế thu hồi những trường hợp không sử dụng, sử dụng sai mục đích, chậm tiến độ hoặc lợi dụng việc sử dụng biển để đầu cơ", đại biểu Trần Văn Lâm lưu ý.
Dự thảo Luật Tài nguyên, môi trường biển và hải đảo (sửa đổi) gồm 6 chương, 76 điều, tập trung quy định về quản lý tổng hợp tài nguyên không gian biển, bảo vệ môi trường biển, hải đảo và quyền, nghĩa vụ, trách nhiệm của các cơ quan, tổ chức, cá nhân có liên quan.
Một nội dung đáng chú ý là hoàn thiện cơ chế quản lý, phân bổ, sử dụng không gian biển. Dự thảo quy định việc giao, cho thuê, đăng ký sử dụng khu vực biển, đấu giá quyền sử dụng và cấp giấy chứng nhận quyền sử dụng khu vực biển, qua đó tạo cơ sở phân bổ nguồn lực công khai, minh bạch, hiệu quả và xử lý xung đột trong sử dụng biển.
Dự thảo hoàn thiện quyền và nghĩa vụ của người sử dụng khu vực biển. Theo đó, có các quyền chuyển nhượng, cho thuê, góp vốn, thế chấp quyền sử dụng khu vực biển và tài sản gắn liền, chuyển mục đích sử dụng, thu hồi, bồi thường, hỗ trợ và nghĩa vụ tài chính.
Các quyền này được thực hiện theo điều kiện, giới hạn phù hợp với quy hoạch, mục đích, thời hạn sử dụng và yêu cầu bảo vệ lợi ích quốc gia, quốc phòng, an ninh, môi trường. Theo Thứ trưởng, đây là cơ sở tạo sự ổn định pháp lý và huy động nguồn vốn lâu dài cho phát triển trên biển.

articles.title: The Problem With Democrats’ Favorite Policy Proposal
articles.text: I f there’s one policy proposal that seems to excite the whole spectrum of Democratic politicians, from insurgent left to establishment moderates, it’s universal child care. The idea, as Senator Elizabeth Warren has put it , is for the government to make day care available “from birth to school age” at little or no cost to parents. Progressives love that it would expand the social safety net and help women balance motherhood with a career. Centrists see it as a concrete way to do something about affordability, while nudging more moms to work and growing the economy in the process. Universal child care is a part of Abdul El-Sayed’s Senate-campaign platform, and Zohran Mamdani has cut ads promising a New York City version. One bill in the House is co-sponsored by former Speaker Nancy Pelosi, the “Squad” member Rashida Tlaib, and the New Jersey arch-moderate Josh Gottheimer. The progressive Roosevelt Institute think tank is all in , as is the more moderate Center for American Progres s. Outside Democratic politics, however, universal child care has limited appeal. Most parents of young children don’t use center-based child care, and they don’t want to. Making day care free, while offering nothing to stay-at-home parents, appeals to the educated, urban, affluent voters who have come to make up the Democratic base, but not to the electorate at large. Universal child care, in other words, might not be the political winner that Democrats seem to think it is. The party’s biggest weakness is that it is widely perceived as out of touch with ordinary Americans. One poll found that most people in swing districts believe that Democrats are focused on helping other people, rather than “people like me.” Universal child care makes the argument for them. The policy has a substantive weakness as well. As an idea, universal child care sounds progressive— universal is right there in the name. But policies that direct considerable resources to the affluent, while offering little for people who need more help, are more aptly described as the opposite. A ccording to the National Center for Education Statistics , just 14 percent of babies younger than 1 year old attend a day-care center. The number rises to 27 percent for kids from 1 to 2 years old. In theory, these low numbers could reflect the fact that parents would like to use day care more, if only they could afford it. But that does not appear to be the case. The liberal think tank New America recently polled 5,000 parents of kids under 6 for a report on their priorities. Only 15 percent of the respondents said their ideal child-care arrangement was exclusively pre-K or day care. (Another 12 percent said they’d like a combination of arrangements that included pre-K or day care). Half wanted to watch the kids themselves or have their partner do it, and another 11 percent would like a relative or friend to do so. [ Kendra Hurley: The biggest obstacle to universal child care: babies ] The desire for subsidized day care finds its most natural constituency in upper-middle-class, dual-earner couples who live in expensive cities, far from their own parents and other relatives. In these families, both parents make too much money to forgo their salary by staying home with a child, but not so much that they don’t feel the pinch of expensive child care. The affluent also have the most to gain, because their communities have the most expensive day cares. Center-based infant care costs more than $30,000 a year in Arlington, Virginia. A few hours southwest, in Buckingham County, Virginia—where there’s far less demand, land is cheap, and wages are low—it costs less than $8,000. American Compass, a socially conservative but economically populist think tank, runs polls on Americans’ ideal family-work arrangement, splitting up the respondents by income. Only among respondents whose household income was above $150,000 was support for “Both parents work full-time, family uses paid child care full-time” above 30 percent. These people are usually Democrats—full-time working mothers of young children voted for Kamala Harris over Donald Trump by a 12-point margin. Stay-at-home mothers of young children voted for Trump over Harris by a 32-point margin. An alternative to subsidizing the behavior of this disproportionately well-off demographic exists: giving cash directly to parents of young children. The nice thing about cash is that it goes to parents without regard for their child-care arrangement—they can use it on day care or a babysitter if they want, or diapers or rent if they don’t. Cash takes no side in the debate over whether kids are better off attending day care or being cared for by a family member. But for some Democratic politicians, that’s actually a drawback: They prefer policies that encourage moms to lean in. In 2012, Pelosi depicted the fight for cheaper child care as the natural evolution of American feminism—a necessary step to “unleash the full power of women.” In a speech earlier this year urging Democrats to run on universal child care, Elizabeth Warren said, “Make this investment so that mamas and daddies can work.” El-Sayed, during a July debate, put it more academically: “For a lot of folks, this has become a gender-justice issue.” This view is reflected in the main universal-child-care plan in Congress: the Child Care for Working Families Act, introduced by Senator Patty Murray and Representative Bobby Scott, and co-sponsored by most Democratic senators and about half of Democratic House members. The bill would cap the cost of child care at 7 percent of a family’s income and have the government pay the rest. To qualify, parents must be employed, or looking for a job, or in school. Stay-at-home moms and dads would receive nothing. (The Trump administration, by contrast, is reported to be working on a rule to allow married stay-at-home parents to claim the Child Care and Development Block Grant, which offers money for child care to low-income families. But the plan seems unlikely to hold up in court, and the grant program is already so underfunded that most currently eligible parents can’t access it.) Some Democrats are willing to meet in the middle, proposing universal child care but also a smaller amount of cash for parents who’d rather take care of their children themselves. Project 2029, an effort by liberal think tankers to make an agenda for the next Democratic administration, features what it calls the Child Care Choice Guarantee, a plan to make available to all parents a spot in a high-quality child-care center for their kid. The plan also proposes a “CareCredit” worth $1,000 a month for families that turn down day care. Last week, Representative Ro Khanna, a potential 2028 presidential candidate, unveiled a similar proposal. A real-life version of this sort of compromise exists in Finland, home of the kind of generous social safety net that American liberals dream of. In Finland, once paid parental leave ends, parents can turn down their guaranteed spot in day care—free or heavily subsidized, depending on family income—in exchange for a modest home-care allowance ranging from about 300 to 700 euros a month. [ Elliot Haspel: Child care is buckling ] According to Tuomas Kosonen, a Finnish economist, the home-care allowance has had an enormous effect. In a 2025 paper , he and his co-authors found that for babies born in 2015 (the last cohort for which it was possible to compile comprehensive data), more than 85 percent of mothers chose the home-care allowance when the child was 10 months old. Even by the child’s second birthday, half of the women were still not back at work. As a result, only 26 percent of Finnish under-3-year-olds were in day care, compared with 59 percent in Denmark and 46 percent in Sweden, neither of which had a comparable allowance. Kosonen is somewhat befuddled by the program’s continued existence. Finland provides affordable, high-quality child care. It is very gender-egalitarian, and outside the period of young motherhood, women there work at a higher rate than they do in most other wealthy countries, the United States included. And yet, according to their revealed preferences, most Finnish moms of young kids would rather stay home and collect a small stipend than go to work to make much more. I asked Scott, the House Democratic sponsor of the Child Care for Working Families Act, how a stay-at-home mother should feel about his bill, which offers her nothing unless she goes to work and puts her kid into day care. Many such parents are not making “a real choice,” he said. “The choice is stay at home or go to work and pay most of your salary to child care, to the point where it’s not worth going to work.” Scott has a point: Many women make the decision to stay home not because they hate working, but because the amount they’d keep after taxes and child-care expenses is small. But there’s another way of looking at it. Whatever would be left after taxes and child care (and it’s usually still tens of thousands of dollars) is what these mothers are forfeiting to stay home with their kids. That’s how strong their preferences are. Democratic politicians and wonks might wish those preferences were otherwise, and they might prefer to subsidize other families who have different ones. But they shouldn’t kid themselves about which category is bigger.

articles.title: Quảng Ngãi nâng công suất mỏ đá phục vụ cao tốc Bắc - Nam
articles.text:
Theo đó, UBND tỉnh Quảng Ngãi cho phép chủ mỏ đá là Công ty TNHH MTV Hoàng Nguyên Hải nâng công suất khai thác năm 2026 thêm 70.000m3 đá nguyên khai, từ 100.000m3 trong giấy phép khai thác lên 170.000m3.
Toàn bộ sản lượng khai thác được phép nâng công suất nói trên phục vụ thi công gói thầu XL2, XL3 giai đoạn II của Dự án thành phần đoạn Quảng Ngãi - Hoài Nhơn, thuộc Dự án Xây dựng công trình đường bộ cao tốc Bắc - Nam phía Đông giai đoạn 2021 - 2025.
Theo UBND tỉnh Quảng Ngãi, động thái trên được thực hiện trên cơ sở mỏ đá Vạn Lý đủ điều kiện nâng công suất, chủ mỏ đề nghị và được Ban Quản lý dự án 2 - Bộ Xây dựng xác nhận.
Mỏ đá Vạn Lý có diện tích khai thác 6ha tại xã Phổ Phong, huyện Đức Phổ (nay là xã Nguyễn Nghiêm) tỉnh Quảng Ngãi. Trữ lượng khoáng sản thiết kế khai thác là gần 2,2 triệu m3.
Dự án thành phần cao tốc Quảng Ngãi - Hoài Nhơn dài 88km, được khởi công từ tháng 1/2023, với tổng mức đầu tư hơn 21.000 tỷ đồng. Tuyến có điểm đầu tại Km1050 (xã Nghĩa Giang, tỉnh Quảng Ngãi), điểm cuối tại Km1138 (phường Bồng Sơn, tỉnh Gia Lai), kết nối trực tiếp với cao tốc Đà Nẵng - Quảng Ngãi ở phía Bắc và cao tốc Hoài Nhơn - Quy Nhơn ở phía Nam để hình thành trục giao thông chiến lược xuyên suốt miền Trung.
Dự án thông xe vào ngày 29/4 vừa qua, hiện chủ đầu tư và liên danh nhà thầu đang tập trung hoàn thành giai đoạn II của dự án, gồm: Nút giao tại Km1092+640, ở phường Đức Phổ và hầm trái 1, 2, 3. Đồng thời, tập trung tháo gỡ vướng mắc, đẩy nhanh tiến độ thi công trạm dừng nghỉ trên tuyến.
